items.title: Maximising capacity utilisation isn't always optimal
items.claim: A factory runs at 95% capacity utilisation. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: This is always the optimal level
Running close to maximum capacity leaves no slack for demand surges, breakdowns or staff absence and tends to raise unit costs through overtime and quality problems
Capacity utilisation has no link to unit cost
Unit costs fall continuously with utilisation

items.reveal:
Hospitals running at >90% bed occupancy have measurably worse patient outcomes (NHS England analyses through the 2010s). Airlines running above 85% load factor face cascading delay risk. Manufacturing plants above 90% have higher defect rates and overtime costs.

Operations researchers use Kingman's formula: waiting time grows non-linearly as utilisation approaches 100%. The textbook assumption that high utilisation is good ignores queueing dynamics.
items.why: Headline utilisation numbers hide trade-offs. The optimal level depends on demand variability, not just on fixed-cost recovery.

items.title: First-mover advantage is more often a myth than a rule
items.claim: Gerard Tellis and Peter Golder studied first movers across 50 product categories. What did they find?

options.text: First movers won permanently in nearly all categories
About 47% of first movers failed and the average market share of survivors was around 10%; long-term winners were more often early followers than pioneers

items.reveal:
Tellis and Golder's 'Will and Vision' (2002) and earlier paper analysed product categories from photocopiers to disposable nappies. Pioneers identified: Chux nappies (replaced by Pampers); WordStar (overtaken by Word); Friendster and MySpace (overtaken by Facebook); AltaVista (overtaken by Google).

Later entrants benefit from market education done by pioneers, technology improvements, and clearer customer preferences. The 'first mover advantage' framing oversells a narrow set of cases (network-effect platforms) as if it were general.
items.why: Business teaching often treats first-mover advantage as a strategic prize. Empirical work suggests being the right mover at the right time is more important than being first.

items.title: Patagonia's owner gave the company to the planet
items.claim: In September 2022, Yvon Chouinard announced he was transferring ownership of Patagonia. What was the structure?

options.text: An IPO on the New York Stock Exchange
All voting stock to the Patagonia Purpose Trust (climate-aligned governance); all non-voting stock (98%) to the Holdfast Collective, with future profits funding environmental causes
A sale to a private equity buyer

items.reveal:
Chouinard, his wife Malinda and their two children transferred Patagonia (valued around $3bn) using two vehicles: the Purpose Trust holds voting control to ensure mission alignment; the Holdfast Collective (a 501(c)(4) nonprofit) holds economic ownership and receives roughly $100m of annual profits to fund environmental work.

The structure required the family to pay $17.5m in gift tax. The company is a B Corp (certified since 2011) — the legal structure goes much further than B Corp certification alone.

B Lab's B Corp movement, launched in 2006, certifies firms meeting social and environmental performance standards.
items.why: Corporate ownership structures shape objectives. A trust-owned firm doesn't have to maximise shareholder returns — because its 'shareholders' are not the same as a public company's.
